title: What is the Oliver Wyman interview process, and how should you prepare?
description: Oliver Wyman's hiring steps: online test, screening interview, case and fit rounds, and the written case used in some offices.
hook: Oliver Wyman usually runs an online application, an online test, a screening interview, a first round of case and fit interviews, and a final round with principals and partners that in some offices adds a written case. Cases are candidate-led and often drawn from real client work, with a tilt towards financial services. Prepare for strong maths, a sharp "why Oliver Wyman" answer and, if your office uses one, the written case.
body:
The stages

Oliver Wyman is a major strategy firm with particular depth in financial services, and its process is known for being thorough. The firm's own interview preparation page describes two kinds of interview, conversational and case. Prep guides and candidate reports add the rest of the shape:

StageWhat usually happens
ApplicationCV and, for many entry-level roles, a cover letter
Online testA short timed test, mostly numerical in some regions; some offices use a work-style questionnaire or add verbal reasoning
Screening interviewA phone or video conversation about your CV and motivation, usually without a case
First roundTypically two interviews, each mixing fit questions with a case
Final roundFurther cases and fit with principals and partners, often on one day; selected offices add a written case

Treat this as the common pattern, not a promise. Office, role and year all change the details, so confirm yours with the recruiter.

What the case interviews test

Oliver Wyman describes the case as an interactive exercise in analytical thinking, often based on real challenges. It lists what it looks for: breaking down an unstructured problem, using data, thinking creatively, applying common sense, asking the right questions and communicating clearly. Its advice is to treat the interviewer as your client and work together.

Cases are generally candidate-led: you build the structure, decide which branch to explore and ask for data. Expect real arithmetic with percentages, margins and growth rates, and expect to be asked what the number means. The firm publishes five practice cases on the same page, including Urban Grocers and Poseidon Water Park. Do all five out loud before your first round.

A worked example: a telematics insurance policy

Prompt: an insurer is thinking of launching a telematics policy for young drivers, priced using data from a device or app that tracks how people drive. Is it worth it?

Step 1: per-policy economics

Assume (illustratively) a premium of $1,000 a year, expected claims of $650, servicing and data costs of $100, and acquisition costs of $120 in the first year.

  • First-year contribution: $1,000 − $650 − $100 − $120 = $130 per policy.
  • Renewal years, with no acquisition cost: $1,000 − $650 − $100 = $250 per policy.
  • At 20,000 policies, the first year contributes 20,000 × $130 = $2.6M before central overhead and capital costs.

Step 2: find the number that matters most

If claims come in 10% higher than expected, at $715, first-year contribution falls to $1,000 − $715 − $100 − $120 = $65. A 10% miss on claims halves the profit. So the real question is whether the telematics data lets the insurer price risk better than competitors, attracting careful young drivers rather than the riskiest ones.

Step 3: say what would change your answer

Claims frequency, fraud, regulation on pricing and data consent, and how many customers renew.

Weak: "Each policy makes $130, so it's profitable and they should launch."
Strong: "It makes about $130 a policy in year one and $250 after that, but a 10% miss on claims halves the first-year figure. I'd launch only if a pilot shows the driving data predicts claims better than our current pricing."

The strong answer finds the sensitive assumption and turns it into a test. That is what partners push on in final rounds. Our guide to unit economics covers this kind of per-customer thinking, and the banking industry guide helps with financial services context.

The written case

Where it is used, you receive a pack with a business scenario and exhibits, work alone for a set time (often around half an hour), then present and defend a recommendation. The trap is reading everything in detail and running out of time. A simple plan for 30 minutes:

  1. 5 minutes: read the question, then skim every page without calculating.
  2. 15 minutes: pick the three or four exhibits that answer the question and do the key calculations.
  3. 7 minutes: write the answer first, then two or three supporting points, a risk and a next step.
  4. 3 minutes: check your numbers and rehearse your first sentence.

Our guide to written and group cases goes further.

Fit and "why Oliver Wyman"

The conversational interviews cover your background, goals and achievements. Prepare four or five stories with real detail. For "why Oliver Wyman", name a practice or type of work, what you learned from someone at the firm, and a link to your own experience. A general interest in financial services is not enough on its own; say which problem in it you want to work on.

Common mistakes

  • Waiting to be led. In a candidate-led case, propose the next step yourself.
  • Reading the whole written pack. Some exhibits are there to test your judgement about what to ignore.
  • Stopping at the number. Say what it means and what would change it.

Practise now

1. Using the telematics numbers above, what is a customer worth over two years if 80% renew?

Show the answer

Year one: $130. Year two: 80% × $250 = $200 on average. Total: $130 + $200 = $330 per customer acquired, before overhead and capital costs.

2. You have 30 minutes and a 14-page written case pack. Ten minutes in, you have read only five pages. What do you do?

Show the answer

Stop reading in detail. Skim the remaining titles and headlines, pick the exhibits that answer the question, and write your recommendation now. A clear answer from four exhibits beats a half-finished analysis of fourteen.

Where to practise next

Work through the complete guide to profitability cases, then practise candidate-led cases from the casebook. Details here were checked in November 2026; processes change by office and year.
